questions.topic: Type I integral as a limit

questions.stem: The integral of e^(-x) from 0 to infinity is improper only because its upper limit is not finite. Define it as the limit of the integral from 0 to b as b grows without bound, and report its value as a number only.

The limit is what makes the definition work: the proper integrals exist for every finite b, and the improper integral exists only when their values settle at a finite number. questions.topic: Condition on a reciprocal-power exponent
questions.learningObjective: state the convergence condition for the reciprocal-power family on an infinite interval
questions.stem: For which values of p does the improper integral of x raised to the power -p, taken from 1 to infinity, converge?

options.text: Exactly when p is greater than 1, since the value is 1 over (p - 1) and that formula is finite only above 1
Exactly when p is at least 1, including the borderline exponent where the antiderivative is a logarithm
options.misconception: includes the borderline exponent, whose logarithm has no finite limit

options.text: Exactly when p is positive, on the grounds that any positive p makes the integrand tend to zero
options.misconception: confuses the integrand tending to zero with the integral converging

options.text: Exactly when p is less than 1, since below that threshold the integrand grows and the area is smaller
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the condition on the exponent

questions.explanation: For p other than 1 the antiderivative of x to the power -p is x to the power (1 - p) over (1 - p), and at infinity that power is negative exactly when p is above 1, so the limit is 0 and the integral is 1 over (p - 1). At p = 1 the antiderivative is the logarithm, and a logarithm has no finite limit at infinity, so that borderline case diverges. The condition is exactly the condition for the p-series to converge, which is the same fact seen from the series side. The trap in the third option is worth naming: an integrand tending to zero is necessary for convergence but nowhere near sufficient, since 1 over x tends to zero and its integral still diverges.
questions.hint: Compute the antiderivative for p other than 1, then handle p equal to 1 separately.

questions.topic: Logarithmic divergence at infinity

questions.stem: Does the improper integral of 1 over (x times the natural logarithm of x), taken from 2 to infinity, converge?

options.text: It converges, since the integrand is smaller than 1 over x and the integral of 1 over x is a familiar convergent shape
options.misconception: cites a benchmark that actually diverges as evidence of convergence

options.text: It diverges, since the integrand is unbounded at the lower limit where the logarithm of 2 is small
options.misconception: attributed the divergence to an endpoint where the integrand is perfectly bounded

options.text: It diverges, since the substitution u equal to the logarithm of x turns it into the integral of 1 over u, which has no limit at infinity

questions.topic: Symmetry claimed across an interior singularity
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the use of odd symmetry across a point where the integrand is undefined
questions.stem: A student writes that the integral of 1 over x from -1 to 1 is 0, because the integrand is odd and the interval is symmetric about the origin. What is wrong with that, and what does the definition of an improper integral actually require?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since an odd integrand over a symmetric interval always integrates to 0 by cancellation
options.misconception: applies odd symmetry across an interval where the integrand is undefined at the centre

options.text: The integral diverges: the one-sided pieces at 0 run to plus infinity and minus infinity, and only a symmetric principal value cancels them
The value 0 is correct but must be computed as one symmetric limit rather than as two one-sided pieces
options.misconception: accepts the value while dropping the two-piece requirement of the definition

options.text: The integral diverges to plus infinity, because only the positive half of the interval contributes a finite area
options.misconception: claims a direction of divergence that the two one-sided pieces do not support

A symmetric cancellation of the two infinities can be arranged, and the result 0 is called the Cauchy principal value, but that is a separate object agreed by convention and not the improper integral. questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Conditional convergence of an improper integral
questions.learningObjective: distinguish conditional from absolute convergence for an improper integral
questions.stem: The improper integral of sin(x) over x from 1 to infinity converges, while the integral of the modulus of sin(x) over x from 1 to infinity does not. What does that pair of facts establish about the first integral?

options.text: It converges conditionally, since it converges while the integral of its modulus fails to converge
It diverges, since an integrand that oscillates without settling cannot have an improper integral
options.misconception: confuses oscillation of the integrand with divergence of the integral

options.text: Both converge, because the modulus of sin(x) is bounded by 1 and a bounded integrand always has a finite integral
options.misconception: believes boundedness of an integrand is enough for a finite integral

options.text: The second converges, because a positive integrand that decays to zero cannot have an infinite integral
options.misconception: believes a positive decaying integrand must give a finite integral

questions.explanation: The two conditions are the definition of the two kinds of convergence for an improper integral, exactly as for a series: the integral converges absolutely when the integral of the modulus converges, and conditionally when the first converges but the second does not. So the sine over x integral is conditionally convergent, its value existing only because the oscillation cancels the positive and negative contributions that the modulus integral accumulates. The cancellation is what makes it exist, and it is also what makes it fragile, since rearranging or chopping the interval changes the value. Note that a positive decaying integrand can certainly diverge, as 1 over x shows, so the last option's premise is simply false.
questions.hint: Compare the definition of absolute convergence with the definition of plain convergence.

questions.topic: Direct comparison with a convergent benchmark
questions.learningObjective: apply direct comparison to decide convergence of an improper integral
questions.stem: A continuous nonnegative function f on the interval from 1 to infinity satisfies the bound f(x) at most 1 over x squared for every x there. What does that bound establish about the integral of f?

options.misconception: makes continuity a requirement of comparison

options.text: The integral of f converges, since f is trapped above by a function whose integral from 1 to infinity is known to be 1
The integral of f diverges, since a function bounded by a decaying reciprocal square cannot itself decay fast enough

options.text: Nothing follows, since the convergence of the bounding integral is itself a claim that would need proving first
options.misconception: refuses to use a benchmark that has in fact already been established

questions.explanation: This is direct comparison, and it works because the bounding integral is known: the reciprocal-square family converges for an exponent above 1, and its value from 1 to infinity is 1. The standard result for a solid hemisphere says the centre of mass sits at 3R over 8 from the flat face, which at R = 2 is also 0.75, so the two agree. questions.topic: A substitution that covers the region twice
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a two-to-one substitution that halves the value of a double integral

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since a change of variables is always permitted and the area of the rectangle must therefore be 1
options.misconception: believes a change of variables is always legitimate and so accepts a wrong area

options.text: The substitution is two to one on the rectangle, so the unit square is covered twice and the value 1 is half of the true area of 2
The Jacobian vanishes on the line x = 0, so the substitution cannot be inverted there and no value is available
options.misconception: blames a vanishing Jacobian, which is a different defect from non-injectivity

options.text: The area is 2 but the substitution has to be applied to the boundary of the region rather than to its interior
options.misconception: believes the change of variables acts on the boundary curve only

questions.explanation: The map x to x squared is not one to one on the interval from -1 to 1, since the values x and minus x give the same u, and the preimage of each u in (0, 1) is the pair of points plus and minus the square root of u. The unit square in the new variables therefore stands for both halves of the original rectangle, and integrating over it once counts each point of the rectangle once rather than twice, which is why the answer came out as 1 rather than 2. There are two repairs and both are standard: restrict to the half where x is at least 0, which gives 1, and then double it, which restores 2. This is the same failure that makes a polar substitution miscount a region that wraps past the axis.
questions.hint: Ask how many original points map to each point of the new region, and check whether the map is one to one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: A Jacobian that vanishes on a line
questions.learningObjective: explain what a vanishing Jacobian rules out for a change of variables
questions.stem: The substitution u = x and v = x y has Jacobian x, which vanishes along the line x = 0. What does that vanishing rule out?

options.text: It rules out describing the image region but leaves the transformed integral itself unaffected
options.misconception: supposes the image can still be used for the integral

options.text: It rules out nothing, since a Jacobian that vanishes on a single line is a routine degeneracy
options.misconception: dismisses the degeneracy as harmless

options.text: It rules out using this map as a smooth invertible coordinate system on any region touching the line x = 0
It rules out the map only where the Jacobian is not constant, since a non-constant Jacobian breaks linearity
options.misconception: confuses a vanishing Jacobian with a non-constant one

questions.explanation: The change-of-variables theorem asks for a map that is continuously differentiable with a non-vanishing Jacobian on the interior of the region, precisely so that the inverse exists there and each point of the image corresponds to one point of the original. A Jacobian that is zero on a line means the map squashes a whole direction to nothing there, so the inverse is not available on any region crossing that line, and the theorem simply does not apply. In practice the response is to split the region into pieces that avoid the line, as the polar substitution is restricted to a half plane when a region would otherwise wrap past the axis. The vanishing is a statement about invertibility, not about linearity or about the image.
questions.hint: Recall what the change-of-variables theorem requires of the Jacobian on the interior of the region.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Why the change of variables must be one to one
questions.learningObjective: explain the one-to-one requirement in the change-of-variables theorem and its failure mode
questions.stem: Explain why a change of variables in a double integral requires the map to be one to one on the region being transformed, and describe what the integral computes when the requirement is not met.

answer.exemplar: The change-of-variables theorem says that the integral of a function over a region equals the integral of the same function composed with the inverse map over the image region, multiplied by the absolute value of the Jacobian, and the two halves of that statement stand or fall together. The inverse map has to exist on the image, which means the map must send each point of the original region to a distinct point of the image, and it must exist smoothly, which is what the non-vanishing Jacobian guarantees. A local inverse is not enough: the map x to x squared on the interval from -1 to 1 has a perfectly good local inverse away from the origin, yet the whole interval is sent onto a single smaller interval, so the image cannot stand for the region. What the integral over the image then computes is the integral over only one sheet of the region, counted once, which is why a two-to-one map typically returns a fraction of the true value. In the example of the rectangle where x runs from -1 to 1 and y runs from 0 to 1, the substitution u equal to x squared and v equal to y sends the rectangle onto the unit square, and integrating with the inverted Jacobian over that square returns 1 instead of the true area of 2, because the two halves of the rectangle are superimposed on one another. The repair is to partition the region into pieces on each of which the map is one to one, treat the images separately, and add the contributions, and that is exactly what one does when a region crosses an axis in polar coordinates and has to be split into two angular pieces. The requirement is therefore not a technicality but the statement that the transformation is a relabelling, and a relabelling that identifies two distinct points is not a relabelling at all.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to show the failure on a concrete computed example and give the partition repair, since merely restating that the map must be one to one would not explain what the integral then computes.
questions.hint: Ask how many original points correspond to each point of the image region, and then ask what the integral over the image therefore measures.

Getting pi over 6 rather than pi over 3 comes from using a quarter turn of azimuth instead of a half turn, which would describe an eighth of the ball.
